plan.contextChunk: This figure shows the logistic sigmoid function sig[z] plotted as a single smooth curve over the range z ∈ [−5, 5]. The horizontal axis is labeled z with tick marks at −5.0, 0.0, and 5.0, and the vertical axis is labeled sig[z] with tick marks at 0.0 and 1.0. A smooth orange S-shaped curve rises monotonically from near zero on the left to near one on the right, with its steepest slope occurring at z = 0 where the function equals exactly 0.5. Gray dashed lines indicate the horizontal asymptote at sig[z] = 1.0 and mark a vertical reference at z = 0, emphasizing the function’s symmetry and its asymptotic approach to both bounds. This figure introduces the logistic sigmoid as a differentiable, bounded activation function that squashes any real-valued input into the interval (0, 1), motivating its use for modeling probabilities in binary classification.

interactionPlan.concept: The logistic sigmoid squashes any real-valued input z into the open interval (0,1) with sig[0] = 0.5 at its point of steepest slope, making it a natural map from scores to probabilities with an invertible decision threshold.
elements: y-axis labeled 'sig[z]' with ticks at 0.0 and 1.0
smooth orange S-shaped sigmoid curve rising monotonically from ~0 at z=-5 to ~1 at z=5
equation annotation '1 / (1 + exp[-z])' in the upper-left plot area
gray dotted horizontal reference line at sig[z] = 0.5 from the y-axis to z = 0
gray dotted vertical reference line at z = 0 from the x-axis to sig[z] = 0.5
draggable marker point on the curve with coordinate readout (z, sig[z])
horizontal threshold line at the slider-chosen probability, with a vertical drop line marking the z intercept where the curve crosses it

interactions.teaches: Every input z maps to exactly one output in (0,1): dragging along the curve reveals that large |z| values saturate near 0 or 1 while inputs near 0 change fastest, so the function compresses extremes and is most sensitive around z = 0

interactions.label: Probability threshold
interactions.teaches: Choosing a probability threshold p is equivalent to choosing a decision boundary on z — the intercept shows that threshold 0.5 corresponds to z = 0, and moving the threshold away from 0.5 shifts the required z monotonically, inverting the sigmoid

demo_steps.title: Shape of the sigmoid
demo_steps.narration: The curve maps any real z to a value strictly between 0 and 1, passing through exactly 0.5 at z = 0 where the dotted reference lines meet. Drag the point along the curve to read off coordinate pairs.

demo_steps.title: Saturation at the extremes
demo_steps.narration: Drag the marker toward z = ±5: the output barely changes near the asymptotes, showing that the sigmoid saturates — large-magnitude inputs all land near 0 or 1.

demo_steps.title: Threshold as a decision boundary
demo_steps.narration: Move the threshold slider: the horizontal line and its z intercept show that classifying by 'sig[z] > p' is the same as thresholding z itself — p = 0.5 gives z = 0, and higher p demands a proportionally larger z.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The sigmoid is a monotonic, invertible squash onto (0,1): a probability threshold on the output is just a shifted threshold on the input, with p = 0.5 exactly at z = 0.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Single orange (salmon/terracotta) S-curve centered in a clean white plot with black spines. Axis labels in italic serif math styling: 'z' below, 'sig[z]' rotated on the left. Equation '1 / (1+exp[−z])' rendered as a stacked fraction in the upper-left interior. Gray dotted crosshair lines at z = 0 and sig[z] = 0.5 always visible; threshold line and its intercept drop-line in a contrasting gray/blue, updating live with the slider. Draggable point snaps to the curve and shows a small '(z, sig[z])' coordinate label beside it.
